title: Regulated Inference Competitive Battlecard (ABM Pilot)
author: Soojin Lee
body:
## Purpose
This battlecard helps AEs/SDRs/SEs win competitive situations for regulated workloads (FinServ + Healthcare) where security review, deployment boundaries (VPC/on-prem), auditability, and predictable performance drive buying decisions.

Use this when a prospect is comparing Redwood Inference to:
- Hyperscalers (managed model endpoints + GPU services)
- LLM API providers (single-vendor hosted APIs)
- Self-hosted stacks (open-source runtime + DIY MLOps)

**What to optimize for in regulated deals:**
1) A security-forward, credible story that accelerates review (SOC2 posture, audit logs, retention/residency, KMS options).
2) A practical deployment path: **Hosted → Dedicated → Private** without rewriting the app.
3) Production economics: latency, throughput predictability, and cost controls that are measurable.

---

## Redwood positioning (regulated workloads)
**Core claim:** Redwood gives teams a single inference platform that can start fast (Hosted), scale predictably (Dedicated), and meet stringent data controls (Private in customer VPC/on-prem), with consistent APIs and operational tooling.

**Win themes to repeat:**
- **Deployment flexibility without re-platforming:** Same API/SDK, consistent model lifecycle controls across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.
- **Auditability + operational controls:** Built for production with per-request observability and audit-friendly operations.
- **Cost/latency predictability:** High-throughput runtime + batching/caching + routing policies to hit SLOs and unit economics.

**What we do NOT lead with:**
- “We are the only compliant option.” (Avoid absolutes.)
- “We support every compliance framework out of the box.” (Be specific, route to approved FAQ.)
- “We never store anything.” (Use approved retention/residency wording; clarify boundaries by deployment mode.)

---

## Competitive landscape: where others win/lose
### 1) Hyperscalers (managed AI endpoints + marketplace models + GPU primitives)
**They win when:**
- The buyer is all-in on a single cloud and values consolidated billing + procurement.
- The workload is already standardized on the hyperscaler’s IAM/networking patterns.
- The prospect wants broad service breadth (data platform + model endpoint + monitoring) rather than best-in-class inference economics.

**They lose / openings for Redwood:**
- **Inference performance tuning is a “you problem”:** getting predictable latency/throughput often requires deep instance, batching, and model-server expertise.
- **Model serving UX is not consistent across deployment modes:** moving from managed endpoint to “private/on-prem” can become a full re-architecture.
- **Opaque unit economics:** cost drivers can be hard to attribute to specific routes/models/prompts.
- **Regulated buyers want clean boundaries:** many regulated teams want a clearly defined inference platform layer with explicit operational responsibilities.

**How to position Redwood:**
- “We integrate into your cloud, but we’re purpose-built for serving and optimizing inference. You get consistent runtime + operational tooling across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.”

### 2) LLM API providers (single-vendor hosted APIs)
**They win when:**
- The buyer prioritizes fastest time-to-demo and is comfortable with a fully hosted SaaS boundary.
- The use case is low-to-moderate volume and security review is lightweight.
- The org can accept vendor-controlled regions/residency and standard retention policies.

**They lose / openings for Redwood:**
- **Private deployment is limited or non-existent:** VPC/on-prem requirements often force a new vendor later.
- **Less control over operational posture:** audit logging, SIEM integration, or tenant isolation may not match regulated expectations.
- **Economics can degrade at scale:** streaming + long contexts + high TPS workloads can become cost surprises.

**How to position Redwood:**
- “You can start hosted with Redwood quickly, but we also give you a clear path to Dedicated and Private when security or scale requires it—without swapping APIs and redoing evaluations.”

### 3) Self-hosted stacks (open model + open-source runtime + DIY orchestration)
**They win when:**
- The org has strong infra/ML platform teams and wants maximum control.
- On-prem/air-gapped is mandatory and they can staff 24/7 operational ownership.
- Procurement is biased toward software-only + internal operation.

**They lose / openings for Redwood:**
- **Time-to-production and reliability:** building SLO-grade inference (autoscaling, rollouts, canaries, fallbacks, observability) takes sustained effort.
- **Security reviews still require evidence:** DIY still needs audit logs, RBAC/SSO integration, operational controls, and documented procedures.
- **Performance tuning is ongoing:** kernel selection, quantization profiles, KV cache strategy, and batching parameters require continuous iteration.

**How to position Redwood:**
- “If you want control without building and operating everything, Redwood Private gives you a supported deployment with clear responsibility boundaries and production-grade serving operations.”

---

## Quick comparison table (talk track)
| Category | Hyperscaler managed endpoints | LLM API providers | Self-hosted stack | Redwood Inference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Time-to-first-call | Fast (in-cloud) | Fastest | Slow-to-medium | Fast (Hosted), then scalable |
| Private/VPC/on-prem | Possible but often complex / fragmented | Often limited | Yes (but DIY) | Yes (Private) |
| Auditability + evidence | Varies by service; can be complex | Varies; often high-level | DIY | Security-forward materials + operational controls |
| Inference economics tuning | Mixed; customer-owned | Vendor-owned but limited knobs | Fully customer-owned | Platform knobs + guidance + observability |
| Operational burden | Medium | Low | High | Low-to-medium (depends on mode) |
| “Same API across modes” | Not typically | N/A | Custom | Yes (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) |

---

## Redwood differentiators to emphasize (regulated deals)
### Differentiator 1: Hosted → Dedicated → Private without re-platforming
**Why it matters:** Regulated teams often need a fast start for evaluation, then a controlled endpoint for production.

**Proof points to mention:**
- Consistent interface and routing policies across deployment modes.
- Rollout controls (canary, A/B, fallback) designed for production serving.

### Differentiator 2: Audit-friendly operational posture
**Why it matters:** In regulated orgs, “security review” is frequently the longest pole.

**Talk track:**
- “We can support security review with questionnaire-ready language and clear boundaries by deployment mode (Hosted vs Private).”
- “We support audit logging and export patterns appropriate for regulated environments.”

**Do:** route to approved addenda.
- FinServ: `abm-finserv-security-faq-addendum`
- Healthcare: `abm-healthcare-security-faq-addendum`

**Don’t:** improvise on retention, logging retention duration, or residency guarantees.

### Differentiator 3: Predictable latency/cost at scale
**Why it matters:** Many regulated use cases (agent assist, summarization, communications review, clinical search) have strict latency and throughput expectations, with high sensitivity to cost variance.

**Talk track:**
- “We make cost/latency drivers visible at the route/model level and provide knobs (batching, caching, routing, quantization profiles) to control unit economics while protecting SLOs.”

### Differentiator 4: Clear responsibility boundaries (especially in Private)
**Why it matters:** Security teams want to know exactly what Redwood operates vs what the customer operates.

**Talk track:**
- “Private deployments are designed with explicit network boundaries, logging pipelines, and KMS integration points. We document shared responsibility clearly.”

---

## Landmine questions to ask early (qualifying + competitive displacement)
These questions uncover whether the prospect will hit blockers with competitors.

### Deployment + data boundaries
1) “Do you require **customer-controlled networking** (VPC/VNet, private connectivity) for production traffic?”
2) “Is **on-prem or air-gapped** a requirement, or just a preference?”
3) “Do you need **data residency** in specific geographies for inference traffic?”

### Security review acceleration
4) “What’s your typical security path: questionnaire → security call → evidence under NDA → pen test review?”
5) “Who owns the decision: CISO/GRC, platform engineering, or app teams?”
6) “Do you require **audit log export** to your SIEM, and what format/transport do you prefer?”

### Reliability + performance reality
7) “What are your p95/p99 latency and throughput targets, and are they uniform or tiered by route?”
8) “How do you handle outages today—do you require fallback to a compatible model/region?”

### Procurement + commercial constraints
9) “Do you need a marketplace purchase path, or can you do a direct vendor agreement?”
10) “Are you trying to avoid GPU procurement and still require VPC-style isolation?”

---

## Competitive traps (what competitors may ask) + recommended responses
### Trap: “Why not just use our cloud’s managed endpoint? It’s already compliant.”
**Response:**
- “If you’re happy with the endpoint performance and operational posture as-is, that can be a good path. Where teams bring us in is when they need consistent inference economics and operational tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments—especially as requirements change during security review or scale-up.”

### Trap: “We can do private networking too.”
**Response:**
- “Private networking is necessary, but regulated teams also need auditability, clear responsibility boundaries, and repeatable rollouts/fallbacks for serving. Redwood Private is built around those operational needs, not just network plumbing.”

### Trap: “Self-hosting is cheaper.”
**Response:**
- “Self-hosting can reduce per-token compute costs in some scenarios, but it shifts cost into engineering time, reliability ownership, and ongoing tuning. We typically see teams underestimate the operational burden of SLO-grade serving and security evidence.”

### Trap: “Your Private offering is just a container—what’s actually included?”
**Response:**
- “Private includes the supported inference platform components needed to run Redwood in your environment with defined operational responsibilities, plus documentation and guidance for network boundaries, logging pipelines, and key management integration. Let’s align on your environment requirements and we’ll map the reference architecture.”

---

## Objection handling by persona
### CISO / Security sponsor
**Objection:** “We can’t send regulated data to a hosted LLM API.”
- “That’s common. Redwood supports Private deployment patterns designed for regulated environments. For evaluation, we can scope the data boundary (synthetic data, redacted payloads, or non-PHI/PCI slices) while we parallel-path the Private requirements.”

**Objection:** “We need audit logs and proof.”
- “Understood. We have questionnaire-ready language and can provide appropriate evidence under NDA. We’ll also align on what audit events you require and how you want exports to your SIEM.”

### GRC / Compliance
**Objection:** “Your answers must match our control language exactly.”
- “We’ll use our approved security FAQ language and map it to your questionnaire controls. If anything is ambiguous, we’ll route it through Security/GRC rather than guessing.”

### Platform engineering
**Objection:** “We don’t want another platform to run.”
- “That’s fair. Redwood is specifically focused on inference serving; we integrate with your existing identity, logging, and networking controls. In Private, we define a clean shared responsibility model so it’s operable, not bespoke.”

### ML engineering
**Objection:** “We need performance knobs and visibility.”
- “We can show token-level latency/cost breakdowns and how batching/caching/routing impacts your workload. We’ll run a short evaluation to establish baseline and tune toward your targets.”

---

## “When to walk away” (or re-scope) guidance
Regulated inference deals can absorb significant time. Use this section to avoid dead-end cycles.

### Walk away / deprioritize if:
- **Mandatory hard requirement** is not supported (e.g., specific air-gapped constraints or non-negotiable commercial terms) and Security/Product confirms no near-term path.
- Prospect insists on **contractual guarantees** we cannot provide (e.g., absolute statements about data handling, unlimited audit log retention, or residency commitments outside supported regions) and won’t accept approved language.
- They require a **single-vendor hyperscaler purchase only**, and explicitly refuse any third-party vendor, even if marketplace paths are available.
- Platform team has already standardized on a self-hosted runtime and is only “pricing checking” with no appetite for vendor-supported operations.

### Re-scope (keep warm) if:
- They need Private eventually, but want to start with Hosted using non-sensitive data to validate performance and API fit.
- They are early in requirements gathering; offer a **security/architecture workshop** with SE + Security to define boundaries and next steps.

**Internal escalation triggers (fast path):**
- Any non-standard retention/residency request
- Any request for SOC reports/evidence without NDA
- Any on-prem/air-gapped request that changes delivery expectations

Owners: Solutions Engineering (Markus Klein) + Security/GRC (Dr. Aisha Rahman / Olga Petrov)

---

## Deal plays (how to win against each category)
### Against hyperscalers
**Play:** “Serving platform, not generic cloud primitives.”
- Ask for their target p95/p99 + TPS + concurrency and who will tune the endpoint.
- Offer a time-boxed evaluation that measures: latency, throughput, unit cost, and operational controls.
- Emphasize consistent API/operations across Dedicated and Private.

### Against LLM API providers
**Play:** “Future-proof the security boundary.”
- Qualify for VPC/on-prem requirement (current or inevitable).
- Emphasize auditability, exportability, and clear boundaries.
- Sell the transition path: start Hosted, graduate to Dedicated/Private without rewriting.

### Against self-hosted
**Play:** “Reduce operational burden, keep control.”
- Validate their staffing/ownership model (on-call, patching, upgrades, scaling, incident response).
- Position Redwood Private as supported, repeatable, and auditable.
- Offer a “build vs buy” total-cost conversation: engineering time + reliability risk + tuning effort.

---

## Proof points and collateral (approved)
Use only approved collateral for regulated prospects.
- Vertical decks: FinServ / Healthcare pitch decks (see related pages)
- Security FAQ addenda: FinServ / Healthcare (questionnaire-ready language)
- Private/VPC reference architecture (network boundaries + logging + KMS integration points)
- Retention/residency positioning guidance (use verbatim language)

---

## Notes for SDRs (email/LI personalization angles)
- “Shortening security review for LLM inference” (lead with auditability + deployment boundaries)
- “Predictable inference cost/latency for customer-facing workflows” (lead with performance + observability)
- “Private deployment path without swapping vendors” (lead with Hosted → Dedicated → Private)

Avoid:
- Naming specific compliance certifications unless you can point to approved language.
- Over-promising data handling statements.
